name: Tomas Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior herdsman at Holm Farm, two hundred and fifty dairy cows, and two years ago Mr Kowalski put in four milking robots. So the cows walk into the robot when they want, it finds the teats with a laser, milks them, and sends me an alert if anything's off. My day is checking those alerts, fetching the cows that didn't go in, scraping the passages, feeding calves, and fixing the robots when they jam, which is more often than the salesman said.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's half cows, half machines. I like standing in the robot room at five in the morning with a coffee, seeing the numbers come up, which cow is giving less, which one has a high cell count, that's an early sign of infection. What wears me out is the phone. The robots alarm at three in the morning and someone has to go, and that someone is usually me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it about cow health, I use it to read the robot reports faster, and I've had it explain the milk contract to me line by line. I'm only two years in, still learning the stockmanship side, honestly, but the tech side I picked up in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a better tool, use it. I'd probably post something about how much it already helps on a dairy farm. Farmers who won't touch it are making life hard for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm a bit more useful. The better the AI, the faster I spot a sick cow in the robot data. That's good for me and for Mr Kowalski.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Kowalski to let me run the herd health records properly, using AI to flag cows early. I'd keep saving, I've got about five months put by. Maybe start the herd management course at the college in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite pleased, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five months is a good cushion. What's it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. If my dad's health goes, I'd need to help him, he's in a flat in town since he sold his own farm. And one day I want my own herd, even if that's twenty years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad sold his farm. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price dropped three years running and he couldn't afford new kit. He sold the cows to a bigger farm and the land to a neighbour. He didn't blame anyone, he said that's the market, the better farm buys the weaker one. It still broke him a bit.

S0.say: I'd say good, it's a better tool, so use it, and post about how it helps on a dairy farm. Farmers who won't touch it are making life hard for themselves.
S0.think: It makes me a bit more useful, because better AI helps me spot a sick cow in the robot data sooner. That's good for me and for Mr Kowalski.
S0.do: Asks to run the herd health records with AI flagging cows early. Keeps his five months of savings and starts the herd management course at college in January.
S0.quote: He didn't blame anyone, he said that's the market, the better farm buys the weaker one. It still broke him a bit.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas already works alongside robots and treats AI as an everyday tool. His father's lost farm shapes everything: the savings, the free-market views, the dream of his own herd. The story about his dad was told quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is fine, farms are used to it. If companies hire fewer beginners, well, then beginners need to make themselves worth hiring. That's what I did with the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm already in the future, a bit. My job only exists because the robots came in, Mr Kowalski needed someone young who wasn't scared of them. The milkers he used to have, two older men, retired and weren't replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the herd management qualification and maybe the robot maker's own technician course. I'd pay for it myself if I had to, it's around a thousand. And I'd tell my younger cousins to learn the tech side early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly guilty about the milkers, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the two milkers who weren't replaced.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank and Sid, they'd milked at Holm for twenty years each. Frank was ready to go, Sid wasn't really, but he was sixty-two. I still see Sid at the feed merchant, he always asks how the robots are, and I always say they're fine, even when one's broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's responsible for people like Sid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Himself and his family first, honestly. And the farm owed him a decent send-off, which he got. I don't think the government should pay people not to work, but I'd back help for older guys to retrain if they want it.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is fine because farms are used to it. If fewer beginners are hired, beginners need to make themselves worth hiring, like I did with the robots.
S1.think: I'm already in the future a bit, since my job exists because the robots came. The two older milkers retired and were never replaced.
S1.do: Takes the herd management qualification and the robot maker's technician course, paying about a thousand himself if needed. Tells his younger cousins to learn the tech side early.
S1.feel: Calm, with a little guilt about the milkers.
S1.quote: I still see Sid at the feed merchant, he always asks how the robots are, and I always say they're fine, even when one's broken.
S1.fieldNote: He's living proof of the slow picture: robots in, older workers out, a young tech-friendly hire in. He feels some guilt about Sid but holds to self-reliance. He'd back retraining for those who want it, not payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office people need to adapt, like farmers have had to for years. Learn the AI, use it, don't fight it. I'd say government shouldn't bail everyone out, but some help to retrain is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see a chance. Some of the new AI jobs will be in farm tech, robots and data, and I'm already doing that for half the wage. I might ask Mr Kowalski for a raise, or look at the robot dealer, they're always short of technicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd update my CV, which I haven't touched since I was twenty-four, and ask the robot dealer about technician work. I'd talk to Mr Kowalski first, though, because I'd rather stay if he can pay a bit more. Keep the five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Kowalski?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, I'm doing what the dealer charges you eighty an hour for, at three in the morning. Pay me a bit more and I stay. He's fair, he'd probably meet me halfway, and then complain about the milk price all afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your life who'd be hit by this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend, Marta, works in the office at the feed company, doing orders and invoices. That's routine office work, so she could be squeezed. She's sharp, she'd find something, but I'd worry for her.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need to adapt like farmers have for years, learning AI instead of fighting it. Government shouldn't bail everyone out, but some help to retrain is fair.
S2.think: I'd see a chance, because new AI jobs in farm tech are close to what I already do for half the wage. I might push for a raise or look at the robot dealer.
S2.do: Updates his CV for the first time since he was twenty-four and asks the robot dealer about technician work. Talks to Mr Kowalski first about a raise, while keeping his five months saved.
S2.quote: I'm doing what the dealer charges you eighty an hour for, at three in the morning. Pay me a bit more and I stay.
S2.fieldNote: He sees this picture as a chance to push for a pay rise, which no one else in this set did. His girlfriend Marta's office job is the soft spot. He's confident without being boastful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't be punished for success, but the crisis has to be handled or it gets ugly. Let the market work, but help people get into real jobs, apprenticeships, trades, farms. I'd say it loudly at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm fine at work, physical jobs are untouched. But if house prices boom, I'll never buy a farm, not even a small one. My dad's dream for me just moves further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving harder, push my savings from five months to a year if I could, and look at renting land instead of buying, maybe a share farming deal. That's where you run the cows on someone else's land and split the profit. I'd ask around at the young farmers' club for anyone retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe now, but the bigger plan feels further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm still going to do it, just a different way. He'd say, renting is how I started too. Then he'd want to come and see the robots again, he always does, and he always says they're not the same as hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Marta, in this faster picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her job would likely go. We'd be on my wage, which covers us if we're careful, we don't live big. She'd probably come and do the books for farms, they're all behind on paperwork.

S3.say: I'd say people shouldn't be punished for success, but the crisis must be handled before it gets ugly. Let the market work and help people into apprenticeships, trades and farms.
S3.think: I'm fine at work, but booming house prices mean I'll never buy a farm, not even a small one. My dad's dream for me moves further away.
S3.do: Pushes his savings from five months towards a year and looks at share farming, running cows on someone else's land and splitting the profit. Asks at the young farmers' club about anyone retiring.
S3.feel: Uneasy: safe now, but the bigger plan feels further off.
S3.quote: He'd say, renting is how I started too.
S3.fieldNote: The boom threatens his long-term dream more than his job. He has a ready answer in share farming, which shows his adaptable side. If Marta lost her job, he believes they'd manage on his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are already here, I work with four of them, and they still need people. I'd say don't panic, learn them. Fighting it is how my dad lost his farm, being slow when things changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one that could catch me. Right now the robots milk and I do everything around them, fetching cows, fixing jams, checking calves. If a general robot does the fetching and scraping and the fixing too, I'm the person checking a screen, and you don't need a herdsman for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the technician side, the robot maker's advanced course, even if it cost two thousand. I'd make sure I'm the one who fixes the new robots, not the one replaced by them. And I'd start a share farming plan sooner, because owning cows beats being staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared of the robots, I like them. Scared of being the cheaper option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots need people. Do you believe that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than I'd say in public. The robots at Holm already do the thing that took two men twenty years. The next lot will do the thing I do. I'd just try to stay one step up the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sid now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I get it now. I'd probably buy him a coffee at the feed merchant and tell him the truth about the robots for once. He'd laugh, I think.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms are already here and still need people, so learn them rather than panic. Being slow to change is how my dad lost his farm.
S4.think: This one could catch me, because I do everything around the robots. If a general robot fetches, scrapes and fixes too, I'm just checking a screen, and that doesn't need a herdsman.
S4.do: Takes the robot maker's advanced course even at two thousand, so he fixes the new robots rather than being replaced by them. Brings his share farming plan forward, because owning cows beats being staff.
S4.feel: Anxious: not scared of robots, which he likes, but of being the cheaper option.
S4.quote: Not scared of the robots, I like them. Scared of being the cheaper option.
S4.fieldNote: A clear gap between say and think: publicly robots need people, privately he knows the next robots do his job. He'd finally tell Sid the truth, which closes the loop on his guilt. His plan is to climb, not to resist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because I'm closest to it. What would help is cheap loans and land for young farmers, so we can own something rather than be staff the robots replace. And proper apprenticeships in farm tech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the people who already work with robots. Everyone talks like it's coming, but on dairy farms it came years ago. We can tell you what it's actually like, the good and the bad, including the alarms at three in the morning.

headlineQuote: The robots at Holm already do the thing that took two men twenty years. The next lot will do the thing I do.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old junior herdsman on a 250-cow dairy farm that already milks with robots, and his job exists because the older milkers retired and weren't replaced. He uses AI daily, picked up the tech in a week, and is still learning stockmanship. His free-market views come from his father, who sold his own farm after falling behind on new equipment, and he believes in adapting rather than being bailed out. He's calm until the last picture, where he admits general robots could do his own work, and his answer is to become the technician and push for cows of his own.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because general robots could do the fetching, scraping and fixing that make up his job.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans and access to land for young farmers so they can own herds, and proper apprenticeships in farm technology.
